headline: Ecuador's Indigenous Community Restores Amazon Through Native Plants
meta_description: In Sarayaku, Ecuador, an Indigenous community has planted over 200,000 native plants and recovered 67 species in two years through women-led nurseries.
summary_short: An Indigenous Ecuadorian community is bringing the Amazon back to life, planting over 200,000 native species and restoring 67 varieties in just two years.
body:
An Indigenous community in Ecuador's Amazon has planted over 200,000 native plants and recovered 67 native species in two years—a remarkable restoration effort driven by women who run seven nurseries dedicated to healing the forest.

Reaching Sarayaku's botanical garden requires a genuine journey. Visitors cross an extensive chakra and navigate a forest trail, where fallen trees and shifting ground mark the path. The effort reflects the community's commitment to place: there are no grand signs announcing arrival, only the appearance of wayuri trees as the slope begins to rise.

This grassroots approach—women-led, locally rooted, focused on native species rather than quick fixes—shows what's possible when Indigenous knowledge meets conservation ambition. The two-year timeline underscores the speed at which native ecosystems can respond when given deliberate, sustained care.
quick_facts: Over 200,000 native plants planted in two years
67 native species recovered by Sarayaku community
Seven women-led nurseries driving restoration efforts
Located in primary forest above Sarayaku river
